items.text: Runs in the radial (spiral) groove on the back of the humerus
items.explain: The radial nerve runs in the radial groove on the posterior humerus, accompanied by the profunda brachii vessels. This explains its vulnerability in mid-shaft humeral fractures.

items.text: Supplies extensor carpi radialis longus
items.explain: The radial nerve supplies extensor carpi radialis longus in the arm, before dividing near the elbow into superficial and deep branches.

items.text: Winds around the surgical neck of the humerus
items.explain: The axillary nerve, not the radial nerve, winds around the surgical neck with the posterior circumflex humeral vessels.

items.text: Is formed from the anterior rami of C7 and C8 only
items.explain: The radial nerve is the continuation of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus and usually contains fibres from C5–T1.

items.text: Injury in the radial groove causes wrist drop
items.explain: A radial nerve lesion in the spiral groove weakens wrist and finger extension and may produce wrist drop; triceps function is often partly preserved.

items.text: Passes behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus
items.explain: The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle in the groove between it and the olecranon, where it is vulnerable to injury.

items.text: Supplies the lateral two lumbricals
items.explain: The ulnar nerve supplies the medial two lumbricals; the lateral two lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve.

items.text: Supplies adductor pollicis
items.explain: Adductor pollicis is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

items.text: Passes deep to the flexor retinaculum through the carpal tunnel
items.explain: The ulnar nerve enters the hand superficial to the flexor retinaculum through Guyon's canal, not through the carpal tunnel.

items.text: It is the most commonly fractured carpal bone
items.explain: The scaphoid is the most frequently fractured carpal bone, commonly after a fall on the outstretched hand.

items.text: Its blood supply enters mainly at the proximal pole
items.explain: Most scaphoid vessels enter distally or dorsally and supply the proximal pole by retrograde flow; the proximal pole is therefore vulnerable to avascular necrosis.

items.text: A fracture through the waist can cause avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment
items.explain: A waist fracture may interrupt the retrograde blood supply to the proximal fragment and lead to avascular necrosis.

items.text: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox suggests a scaphoid fracture
items.explain: Anatomical snuffbox tenderness after a fall is a classic clinical sign that raises suspicion of scaphoid fracture.

items.text: It articulates with the ulna
items.explain: The scaphoid articulates with the radius, lunate, capitate and trapezium/trapezoid region, not the ulna.

items.text: It has three lobes
items.explain: The right lung has superior, middle and inferior lobes, separated by horizontal and oblique fissures.

items.text: It has a cardiac notch
items.explain: The prominent cardiac notch is a feature of the left lung; the right lung does not have a comparable cardiac notch.

items.text: It has an oblique and a horizontal fissure
items.explain: The right lung has both an oblique fissure and a horizontal fissure.

items.text: Its main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical than the left
items.explain: The right main bronchus is generally shorter, wider and more vertical than the left, which is why aspirated objects more often enter it.

items.text: It has a lingula
items.explain: The lingula is part of the left upper lobe and is not present in the right lung.

items.text: Granular cells secrete renin
items.explain: Juxtaglomerular (granular) cells are modified smooth muscle cells, mainly in the afferent arteriole, and secrete renin.

items.text: Macula densa cells secrete renin
items.explain: Macula densa cells detect tubular sodium chloride delivery and signal nearby granular cells; they are not the principal renin-secreting cells.

items.text: The macula densa senses sodium chloride delivery in the distal tubule
items.explain: Macula densa cells monitor sodium chloride concentration and flow in tubular fluid near the end of the thick ascending limb and early distal tubule.

items.text: Granular cells are modified smooth muscle cells of the efferent arteriole
items.explain: Granular cells are modified smooth muscle cells chiefly associated with the afferent arteriole, not the efferent arteriole.

items.text: The descending limb is highly permeable to water
items.explain: The thin descending limb is highly permeable to water, allowing water to leave as the tubular fluid descends into the increasingly hyperosmotic medulla.

items.text: The thick ascending limb is permeable to water
items.explain: The thick ascending limb is essentially impermeable to water, while reabsorbing sodium, potassium and chloride.

items.text: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs sodium through the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter
items.explain: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs Na+, K+ and 2Cl− via the apical Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2).

items.text: Loop diuretics such as furosemide block this cotransporter
items.explain: Loop diuretics such as furosemide inhibit NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, reducing NaCl reabsorption and the medullary osmotic gradient.

items.text: Fluid entering the distal tubule is hypertonic to plasma
items.explain: Fluid leaving the water-impermeable thick ascending limb is dilute, so early distal tubular fluid is typically hypotonic to plasma.

questions.q: About glomerular filtration rate and clearance:

items.text: Inulin clearance can be used to measure GFR
items.explain: Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals the glomerular filtration rate.

items.text: A normal GFR in a healthy adult is about 125 mL/min
items.explain: A commonly cited average GFR in a healthy young adult is approximately 125 mL/min, with variation by body size, age and sex.

items.text: Creatinine is freely filtered and not reabsorbed
items.explain: Creatinine is freely filtered and is not significantly reabsorbed, although a small amount is secreted by renal tubules.

items.text: The clearance of glucose in a healthy person equals the GFR
items.explain: In a healthy person, filtered glucose is normally reabsorbed almost completely, so its clearance is approximately zero rather than equal to GFR.

items.text: The hypothalamus is the main integrating centre for temperature control
items.explain: The hypothalamus integrates thermoregulatory information and coordinates autonomic, behavioural and endocrine responses.

items.text: Sweating is stimulated by sympathetic cholinergic fibres
items.explain: Most eccrine sweat glands are activated by sympathetic postganglionic fibres that release acetylcholine.

items.text: Shivering is triggered when core temperature rises
items.explain: Shivering is a heat-generating response to cold; it is triggered when body temperature falls below the defended range.

items.text: When air temperature is above skin temperature, evaporation is the main route of heat loss
items.explain: When air temperature exceeds skin temperature, radiation and convection may add heat to the body; evaporation becomes the principal avenue for net heat loss.

items.text: The fibres are multinucleated
items.explain: Skeletal muscle fibres are long cylindrical cells formed by fusion of myoblasts and therefore contain multiple nuclei.

items.text: The nuclei lie at the periphery, just under the sarcolemma
items.explain: In mature skeletal muscle, nuclei are typically located peripherally beneath the sarcolemma.

items.text: Intercalated discs are a feature of skeletal muscle
items.explain: Intercalated discs are characteristic of cardiac muscle, not skeletal muscle.

items.text: The fibres show cross-striations
items.explain: Skeletal muscle shows cross-striations due to the regular arrangement of actin and myosin filaments into sarcomeres.

items.text: The fibres are branched
items.explain: Skeletal muscle fibres are generally long and unbranched; branching is characteristic of cardiac muscle cells.
